Doctor: Good morning. So you're a 29-year-old female coming in for your routine prenatal visit, and by my count you're 28 weeks today. How have you been feeling?
Patient: Pretty good, honestly. I get tired in the afternoons, but I have a toddler at home, so I figured that's normal.
Doctor: That's very common. Any headaches, changes in your vision, or swelling in your face or hands?
Patient: No headaches and no vision changes. My ankles get a little puffy at night, but it's gone by morning.
Doctor: Okay. Any bleeding, leaking of fluid, or contractions?
Patient: No bleeding, no leaking, and no real contractions. Just some Braxton Hicks tightening now and then.
Doctor: And is the baby moving well?
Patient: Yes, every day, especially after dinner.
Doctor: Any burning when you urinate?
Patient: No.
Doctor: What are you taking right now?
Patient: Just my prenatal vitamin once a day.
Doctor: Good. Your blood pressure today is 112 over 68 and your weight is up about 18 pounds from before the pregnancy. Your urine dip shows no protein and no glucose. Let me measure your belly. Fundal height is 28 centimeters, which matches your dates, and the baby's heart rate by Doppler is 146 beats per minute.
Patient: That sounds good.
Doctor: Your one-hour glucose challenge test from last week came back at 118, which is normal, so no gestational diabetes. Your hemoglobin was 10.4, which is a little low, so you have mild anemia of pregnancy. Your blood type is O positive, so you won't need the Rh immune globulin shot.
Patient: Should I do something about the anemia?
Doctor: Yes, I'd like you to start ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily, and keep taking the prenatal vitamin. It can cause constipation, so drink plenty of water. We'll recheck your hemoglobin in four weeks. I also recommend the Tdap vaccine today, since this is the right window in the third trimester.
Patient: Okay, I'll take it.
Doctor: To summarize, you're progressing normally at 28 weeks with mild anemia of pregnancy and some mild ankle swelling that is normal for this stage. Start the iron, Tdap today, repeat hemoglobin in four weeks, and I'll see you back in two weeks. Call us right away for headaches, vision changes, bleeding, leaking fluid, decreased movement, or regular contractions.
Patient: Will do, thank you.
summary: A 29-year-old female presented for a routine prenatal visit at 28 weeks, reporting afternoon tiredness and mild ankle puffiness at night while denying headaches, vision changes, bleeding, leaking fluid, and real contractions. Blood pressure was 112 over 68, fundal height matched dates at 28 centimeters, and the fetal heart rate was 146 beats per minute. The one-hour glucose challenge test was normal at 118, but hemoglobin was low at 10.4, consistent with mild anemia of pregnancy. The plan is to start ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily, continue the prenatal vitamin, give the Tdap vaccine today, recheck hemoglobin in four weeks, and return in two weeks.

soap.subjective: Routine prenatal visit at 28 weeks. Reports tiredness in the afternoons and ankles that get a little puffy at night but resolve by morning, with occasional Braxton Hicks tightening. Denies headaches, vision changes, bleeding, leaking of fluid, real contractions, and burning when urinating. The baby moves daily. Takes a prenatal vitamin once a day.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 112 over 68; weight up about 18 pounds from before the pregnancy. Urine dip negative for protein and glucose. Fundal height 28 centimeters, matching dates. Fetal heart rate by Doppler 146 beats per minute. One-hour glucose challenge test 118 (normal). Hemoglobin 10.4 (low). Blood type O positive.
soap.assessment: Normal progress at 28 weeks of pregnancy with mild anemia of pregnancy and mild ankle swelling that is normal for this stage; no gestational diabetes.

Counsel to drink plenty of water because iron can cause constipation
Give the Tdap vaccine today
Recheck hemoglobin in four weeks
Rh immune globulin not needed because blood type is O positive
Return visit in two weeks
Call right away for headaches, vision changes, bleeding, leaking fluid, decreased movement, or regular contractions

Doctor: Hi there. I understand we have a 6-year-old female here with ear pain. Can you tell me what's been going on?
Family member: She woke up crying two nights ago holding her right ear, and yesterday she had a fever and was really fussy. She keeps pulling at it.
Doctor: Did you check her temperature at home?
Family member: Yes, it was 101 yesterday evening. I gave her ibuprofen and that helped for a few hours.
Doctor: Any vomiting, diarrhea, rash, or stiff neck?
Family member: No vomiting, diarrhea, rash, or stiff neck. She's been drinking okay but she's not eating much.
Doctor: Any drainage coming out of the ear, or trouble hearing?
Family member: No drainage. She says sounds are muffled on that side.
Doctor: Any sore throat or cold symptoms?
Family member: A little sore throat yesterday. She's had a runny nose and a stuffy nose for about a week. She also has seasonal allergies and takes cetirizine 5 mg every morning.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Family member: No, none.
Doctor: Okay. Her vitals today are temperature 38.4 Celsius, heart rate 104, respiratory rate 22, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She weighs 20 kilograms. Let me look in her ears. The left eardrum looks normal. The right eardrum is red and bulging with pus behind it, and it doesn't move when I puff air at it. Tympanometry on the right is flat, which fits with fluid. Her throat is mildly red with no exudate, her neck is supple, and her lungs are clear. I also did a rapid strep swab, and it was negative.
Family member: So is it an ear infection?
Doctor: Yes, this is an acute otitis media of the right ear. Because she has a fever and significant pain, I'm starting amoxicillin 900 mg by mouth twice a day for 10 days. Keep giving ibuprofen 200 mg every six hours as needed for pain or fever, and continue the cetirizine. She should improve within 48 to 72 hours. Call us if she's not better by then, or if she gets worse ear pain, swelling behind the ear, or a high fever. We'll recheck her ears in about two weeks to make sure the fluid has cleared.
Family member: Okay. Can she go to school?
Doctor: Once she's been fever-free for 24 hours, yes.
summary: A 6-year-old female presented with two days of right ear pain, fever, and fussiness, along with a week of runny and stuffy nose and a mild sore throat, while her family denied vomiting, diarrhea, rash, stiff neck, and ear drainage. Temperature was 38.4 Celsius, the right eardrum was red and bulging with flat tympanometry, and a rapid strep swab was negative. She was diagnosed with acute otitis media of the right ear and also has seasonal allergies treated with cetirizine. The plan is amoxicillin 900 mg twice a day for 10 days, ibuprofen as needed, continued cetirizine, and an ear recheck in about two weeks.

Left eardrum normal; right eardrum red and bulging with pus behind it and no movement with air puff. Right tympanometry flat. Throat mildly red without exudate, neck supple, lungs clear. soap.assessment: Acute otitis media of the right ear; seasonal allergies.

Ibuprofen 200 mg every six hours as needed for pain or fever

Doctor: Hello, what brings you in today?
Patient: My acne has gotten a lot worse over the last month, mostly along my jawline and chin. It's the worst it's been since college.
Doctor: I see. So you're a 28-year-old female with acne that has flared over the last month. What have you been using for it?
Patient: Tretinoin cream, 0.025 percent, at bedtime, and spironolactone 50 mg once a day, which my last doctor started about six months ago. And a benzoyl peroxide wash, 4 percent, in the shower.
Doctor: Was that working?
Patient: It was working until about a month ago. Now I have new painful bumps on my chin and jaw. No scarring that I can see, and no cysts that drain.
Doctor: Any fever, joint pain, or rash anywhere else on your body?
Patient: No fever, no joint pain, and no rash anywhere else.
Doctor: Is there any chance you could be pregnant? When was your last period?
Patient: Actually, it's been about eight weeks. I've been nauseous in the mornings and my breasts are tender. I hadn't thought of it with all the acne.
Doctor: Okay, that matters a lot for which medicines we can use. Are you on birth control?
Patient: No, we weren't using anything.
Doctor: Any allergies to medications?
Patient: None.
Doctor: Let's do a urine pregnancy test right now.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: The urine pregnancy test is positive, so you're pregnant.
Patient: Oh wow. We were hoping for this, just not this quickly. Is my acne medicine safe?
Doctor: Not all of it. Let me examine you. Your blood pressure is 108 over 66 and your heart rate is 76. On your face I see about 15 inflammatory papules and a few pustules along the jawline and chin, with a few comedones on the forehead. No nodules, no cysts, and no scarring.
Doctor: So this is acne vulgaris, moderate, and it is probably worsened by pregnancy hormones. Because you're pregnant, I'm stopping the spironolactone and the tretinoin cream today, since neither is recommended in pregnancy. We'll start azelaic acid 15 percent gel twice a day, which is considered safe. You can continue the benzoyl peroxide wash once daily. Please avoid oral isotretinoin and doxycycline for the rest of your pregnancy. I'd also like you to start a prenatal vitamin once daily and call your obstetrician this week to book your first prenatal visit.
Patient: Okay. How long until my skin improves?
Doctor: Probably six to eight weeks. We'll see you back in eight weeks to check how it's responding.
summary: A 28-year-old female presented with a month of worsening acne along the jawline and chin despite tretinoin cream, spironolactone, and a benzoyl peroxide wash, and she also reported about eight weeks since her last period, morning nausea, and tender breasts. She denied fever, joint pain, and rash elsewhere. A urine pregnancy test was positive, vital signs were stable, and examination showed inflammatory papules and pustules without nodules, cysts, or scarring. The assessment was moderate acne vulgaris likely worsened by pregnancy. The spironolactone and tretinoin were stopped, azelaic acid gel was started, and she was advised to start a prenatal vitamin and call her obstetrician this week.

No scarring, draining cysts, fever, joint pain, or rash elsewhere. Last period about eight weeks ago with morning nausea and tender breasts; no birth control in use. No medication allergies.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 108 over 66, heart rate 76. Urine pregnancy test positive. About 15 inflammatory papules and a few pustules along the jawline and chin, a few comedones on the forehead; no nodules, no cysts, no scarring.
soap.assessment: Acne vulgaris, moderate, probably worsened by pregnancy hormones; patient is pregnant.
plan: Stop spironolactone and tretinoin cream because neither is recommended in pregnancy
Start azelaic acid 15 percent gel twice a day
Continue benzoyl peroxide wash once daily
Avoid oral isotretinoin and doxycycline for the rest of the pregnancy
Start a prenatal vitamin once daily
Call obstetrician this week to book the first prenatal visit
Expect improvement in six to eight weeks; return in eight weeks

Hospital day 2 progress note for a 55-year-old male admitted with cellulitis of the right lower leg. He reports that the pain and warmth in his shin have improved since admission and that the redness has stopped spreading. He denies fever, chills, nausea, or vomiting overnight, and he denies chest pain and shortness of breath. He continues to smoke about one pack of cigarettes per day and describes his nicotine cravings as manageable so far, but he is open to help quitting.

Overnight there were no acute events. His only scheduled medication is cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours. Vital signs this morning: temperature 37.2 Celsius, heart rate 78, blood pressure 128/80, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On examination, the erythema over the anterior right shin has shrunk compared with the margin marked on admission, with mild warmth, mild tenderness, and trace edema. There is no fluctuance, no drainage, and no crepitus, the calf is soft, and distal pulses are palpable. The white blood cell count is 10.8 today, down from 14.2 on admission, and blood cultures drawn on admission show no growth after two days.

Impression: right lower leg cellulitis, improving on IV antibiotics, and ongoing tobacco use.

Plan is to continue cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours today, keep the leg elevated, and re-mark the borders of the erythema each shift. If he stays afebrile and the redness continues to recede, we will switch to an oral antibiotic tomorrow and plan discharge. I counseled him on smoking cessation, and he agreed to try a nicotine patch 14 mg daily, which I ordered today. We will recheck the white blood cell count in the morning.
summary: A 55-year-old male on hospital day 2 for right lower leg cellulitis reported improved pain and warmth and denied fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Vital signs were stable, the erythema had shrunk from the admission margin, and the white blood cell count fell from 14.2 to 10.8 with blood cultures showing no growth. The impression was improving cellulitis and ongoing tobacco use. The plan is to continue IV cefazolin, elevate the leg, start a nicotine patch, and consider oral antibiotics and discharge tomorrow.

Hospital day 3 progress note for a 48-year-old male admitted with severe retrosternal burning and regurgitation despite daily proton pump inhibitor therapy, now followed by gastroenterology for refractory gastroesophageal reflux disease. He works rotating night shifts at a distribution center, and his sleep and meal times shift from week to week. On working nights he typically eats a large meal around 3 am, and after his shift ends he goes to bed within an hour and sleeps flat during the day, which likely contributes to his symptoms.

Interval events: A cardiac cause was excluded on admission with two negative troponin measurements and a normal ECG. He underwent EGD yesterday, which showed LA grade B erosive esophagitis and a 3 cm hiatal hernia without Barrett's changes, and biopsies were taken from the distal esophagus and the stomach. He tolerated the procedure well. His burning chest pain is somewhat better today at 3 out of 10, compared with 8 out of 10 on admission. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, hematemesis, melena, fever, and unintentional weight loss. He has not had any exertional chest pain.

Medication reconciliation: On admission he told the team that he takes omeprazole 40 mg twice daily at home. His wife brought in his bottles today, and the label reads omeprazole 20 mg once daily, so correction, his home dose is omeprazole 20 mg once daily, not 40 mg twice daily. He takes it at irregular times, often with or after his first meal, and skips it on rushed nights. His reflux therefore persisted on low-dose once-daily therapy and not on maximal twice-daily therapy. Other home medications are lisinopril 20 mg daily for HTN, metformin 1000 mg twice daily for T2DM, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly for hyperlipidemia, and famotidine 20 mg at bedtime as needed. He also admits to taking ibuprofen 400 mg a few times a week for low back pain from lifting at work. He has no known drug allergies.

Current inpatient medications: pantoprazole 40 mg IV once daily since admission, along with his lisinopril, metformin, and atorvastatin.

Vital signs: Temp 36.9 C, HR 76, BP 138/84, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air. Weight 104 kg, BMI 34, consistent with obesity. He is comfortable on exam. The abdomen is obese and soft with mild epigastric tenderness and no guarding or rebound. Lungs are clear. There is no edema. Labs this morning: WBC 7.2, Hgb 14.2, Na 139, K 4.1, Cr 0.9, glucose 148. HbA1c from admission was 7.4%.

Impression: Refractory GERD with LA grade B erosive esophagitis and a 3 cm hiatal hernia. Contributors are his rotating night schedule with large late meals before lying flat, obesity, regular ibuprofen use, and suboptimal PPI use (low dose, once daily, and poorly timed). HTN, T2DM, and hyperlipidemia are stable.

Recommendations: Increase pantoprazole to 40 mg IV twice daily today, then transition to oral esomeprazole 40 mg twice daily at discharge, taken 30 minutes before his first meal after waking and again before his second main meal of the day, whatever clock time that falls at. Discontinue home omeprazole. Stop ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for back pain instead. Continue famotidine 20 mg at bedtime, taken before his daytime sleep period. Continue lisinopril, metformin, and atorvastatin without changes.

I counseled him to avoid eating within 3 hours of lying down, to eat smaller meals, to keep a consistent meal schedule anchored to his wake time, and to raise the head of the bed by 6 inches. A dietitian referral for meal planning around shift work and weight loss will be placed. We will follow up the esophageal and gastric biopsy pathology for Barrett's esophagus, eosinophilic esophagitis, and H. pylori. If symptoms persist after 8 weeks of twice-daily therapy, he will need 24-hour pH-impedance monitoring and referral for surgical evaluation of antireflux surgery. He is likely ready for discharge tomorrow if his pain remains controlled and he tolerates his diet. GI clinic follow-up in 6 to 8 weeks.
summary: A 48-year-old male night-shift worker on hospital day 3 for refractory gastroesophageal reflux disease had EGD showing LA grade B erosive esophagitis and a 3 cm hiatal hernia, after a cardiac cause was excluded. Medication reconciliation corrected his home PPI to omeprazole 20 mg once daily taken at irregular times, not 40 mg twice daily. He also takes ibuprofen for back pain, and he has HTN, T2DM, hyperlipidemia, and obesity. Pantoprazole is being increased to 40 mg IV twice daily with transition to oral esomeprazole 40 mg twice daily, and omeprazole and ibuprofen are stopped. Biopsy follow-up, lifestyle and dietitian counseling, and pH-impedance testing if symptoms persist were planned.

EGD: LA grade B erosive esophagitis and 3 cm hiatal hernia without Barrett's changes; biopsies taken. WBC 7.2, Hgb 14.2, Na 139, K 4.1, Cr 0.9, glucose 148, HbA1c 7.4%.
soap.assessment: Refractory GERD with LA grade B erosive esophagitis and a 3 cm hiatal hernia, contributed to by rotating night shifts with late large meals before lying flat, obesity, regular ibuprofen use, and suboptimal PPI use. HTN, T2DM, and hyperlipidemia are stable.

Discontinue home omeprazole

Doctor: Good afternoon. So you're a 56-year-old male here about a rash. When did this start?
Patient: About five days ago I got this burning, stabbing pain on my left side, under my arm and around toward my back. Three days ago the rash came up.
Doctor: Has the rash spread across the midline or anywhere else?
Patient: No, it's all in a band on the left side. It's blisters mostly, and it hurts to even have my shirt touch it.
Doctor: Any fever, headache, or changes in your vision?
Patient: No fever, no headache, nothing with my eyes.
Doctor: Any weakness in your arm or leg, or trouble passing urine?
Patient: No weakness and no trouble with urine.
Doctor: Have you had chickenpox before, or the shingles vaccine?
Patient: I had chickenpox as a kid. I never had the vaccine.
Doctor: Any medical conditions or medicines I should know about?
Patient: High blood pressure, and I take lisinopril 10 mg every day. No allergies to medicines.
Doctor: I need to ask about alcohol. How much are you drinking?
Patient: Honestly, about six beers a day, sometimes more on weekends. My last drink was this morning.
Doctor: Thank you for being open about that. That is heavy alcohol use, and it affects how we treat this. Any shakiness, sweating, or seeing things that aren't there when you go without a drink?
Patient: I get shaky in the mornings sometimes, but no sweats and no hallucinations.
Doctor: Your vitals today are blood pressure 146/90, heart rate 94, temperature 37.0 Celsius, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On exam there are grouped vesicles on a red base in a band along the left T6 dermatome, from just below the armpit to the middle of your back. Some are crusting, and none are on your face or near your eye. There's no tremor today, and you're alert and oriented. Blood work from your primary doctor last month showed a creatinine of 0.9, AST 64, and ALT 40.
Patient: So is it shingles?
Doctor: Yes, this is herpes zoster, or shingles. Because the rash is only three days old, the antiviral should help, so I'm starting valacyclovir 1000 mg three times a day for seven days. For the nerve pain I'm starting gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime, a low dose because alcohol adds to the drowsiness. You can take acetaminophen 500 mg every six hours as needed, but no more than 2 grams a day because of your drinking. Please avoid ibuprofen and similar pain relievers. I'm also starting thiamine 100 mg once daily, and I'm ordering a hepatic panel today. Keep the blisters covered, since you can pass the virus to anyone who hasn't had chickenpox.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: Please try to cut back on alcohol, but don't stop suddenly because of the withdrawal risk. I'd like to connect you with our addiction counselor to plan a safe reduction. Return in one week, or sooner if the rash spreads to your face, your eye hurts, or you get a fever. After you recover we'll talk about the shingles vaccine.
summary: A 56-year-old male with hypertension and heavy alcohol use presented with five days of burning, stabbing left-sided pain and a blistering band-like rash for three days, denying fever, headache, eye symptoms, and weakness. Blood pressure was 146/90, and examination showed grouped vesicles along the left T6 dermatome without facial involvement or tremor. He was diagnosed with herpes zoster and started on valacyclovir 1000 mg three times a day for seven days, gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime, acetaminophen limited to 2 grams a day, and thiamine, with ibuprofen avoided. A hepatic panel was ordered, alcohol reduction counseling was arranged, and he will return in one week.

soap.subjective: Five days of burning, stabbing pain on the left side from under the arm toward the back, followed three days ago by a blistering rash in a band on the left side that hurts to touch. No fever, headache, vision or eye symptoms, weakness, or trouble with urine. Had chickenpox as a child and never had the shingles vaccine. Has high blood pressure on lisinopril 10 mg every day; no medication allergies. Drinks about six beers a day, last drink this morning; gets shaky in the mornings sometimes but denies sweats and hallucinations.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 146/90, heart rate 94, temperature 37.0 Celsius, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Grouped vesicles on a red base in a band along the left T6 dermatome from below the armpit to the mid back, some crusting; none on the face or near the eye. No tremor, alert and oriented. Recent labs from the primary doctor: creatinine 0.9, AST 64, ALT 40.
soap.assessment: Herpes zoster in the left T6 dermatome, early (rash three days old); high blood pressure; heavy alcohol use.

Start gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime at a low dose because alcohol adds to drowsiness

Doctor: Hi, thanks for coming in. I understand you're a 70-year-old male here because of some trouble with your memory. What's been happening?
Patient: Well, my daughter made me come. A couple of days ago I got lost driving home from the grocery store, one I've gone to for twenty years. I figured it out after a while, but it scared me.
Family member: He's been forgetting things for about a year, Doctor. He repeats the same questions and misplaces his keys and wallet. He's also missed a couple of bill payments, which he never used to do.
Doctor: Has it been getting worse quickly, or slowly over time?
Family member: Slowly. It's more noticeable this last year.
Doctor: Any head injury or falls recently?
Patient: No falls, and I haven't hit my head.
Doctor: Any headaches or weakness?
Patient: No headaches, no weakness.
Doctor: What about your mood? Any sadness, or seeing things that aren't there?
Patient: I'm a little down about this, but I'm not depressed, and no, I don't see things.
Family member: And he sleeps poorly, so he takes something every night to help.
Doctor: What do you take?
Patient: Diphenhydramine, 50 mg at bedtime, the store-brand version of Benadryl. I also take lisinopril 10 mg every morning for blood pressure and tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily for my prostate.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Your vitals today are blood pressure 136/78, heart rate 72, temperature 36.8 Celsius, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Your fingerstick glucose is 104. On exam you're alert and pleasant, your heart and lungs sound normal, there's no weakness, your speech is fluent, and your walking is steady. On the memory screen, the MoCA, you scored 23 out of 30, with most of the points lost on delayed recall and the clock drawing.
Patient: Is that bad?
Doctor: It's mildly low. A slow decline over a year with you still mostly independent in daily activities fits mild cognitive impairment. That is not the same as dementia. Some things can make memory worse, and diphenhydramine is a big one in older adults, so I'd like you to stop it. You can try melatonin 3 mg at bedtime instead. Continue the lisinopril and tamsulosin. Urgent care isn't the place for the full workup, so I'm ordering blood tests today, a vitamin B12 level, TSH, a complete metabolic panel, and a CBC, and I'm referring you for an MRI of the brain and to our geriatrics clinic for a full memory evaluation. Until then, please don't drive alone on unfamiliar routes, and have your daughter help with the bills.
Family member: Okay, we'll do that.
Patient: All right. Thank you.
summary: A 70-year-old male came to urgent care with his daughter after getting lost driving home from a familiar store, with about a year of slowly progressive forgetfulness, repeated questions, misplaced items, and missed bill payments. He denied falls, head injury, headaches, weakness, and depression, and he takes diphenhydramine nightly for poor sleep. Vital signs were normal, fingerstick glucose was 104, the neurologic exam was nonfocal, and the MoCA score was 23 out of 30. The impression was mild cognitive impairment, and diphenhydramine was stopped in favor of melatonin. Blood tests, a brain MRI, and a geriatrics referral were ordered, with advice not to drive alone on unfamiliar routes.

note:
Reason for consult: Positive interferon-gamma release assay in a 46-year-old female; evaluation and treatment recommendations for latent tuberculosis infection. Requesting service: Emergency Medicine. A professional Spanish medical interpreter (video) was used for the entire interview and examination.

HPI: The patient is a 46-year-old female who works as a home health aide. Her employer's health program found a positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold test on routine screening this week and sent her to the emergency department for a same-day chest radiograph. She reports a mild dry cough for about two weeks that began after a cold. She denies fever, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, hemoptysis, chest pain, and shortness of breath. She has no known contact with anyone who has active tuberculosis. She was born in Central America and moved to the United States 12 years ago. She was never treated for tuberculosis and does not recall a prior skin test.

Past medical history: Hypothyroidism. No history of liver disease, diabetes, or HIV. Medications: levothyroxine 75 mcg daily and oral contraceptive pills. Allergies: no known drug allergies. Social history: Lives with her husband and two children. Drinks alcohol rarely, no tobacco use, and no injection drug use.

Examination: Temperature 36.8 Celsius, heart rate 78, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, weight 62 kg. She appears well. There is no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. Heart rhythm is regular. The abdomen is soft and non-tender without hepatomegaly.

Data reviewed: The interferon-gamma release assay is positive. The ED chest radiograph shows clear lung fields with no infiltrate, cavitation, or hilar adenopathy. Liver enzymes are normal, with AST 24 and ALT 22. HIV antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody are all negative.

Impression: Latent tuberculosis infection in a patient with a normal chest radiograph. Her mild dry cough is most consistent with a resolving viral illness, and the likelihood of active tuberculosis is low, but sputum testing is reasonable before starting treatment because of the cough.

Recommendations:
1. Collect two sputum samples for AFB smear and culture before the first dose.
2. Once both smears return negative, start rifampin 600 mg by mouth once daily for four months.
3. Counsel through the interpreter that rifampin turns urine and tears orange and can reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptive pills. Recommend a non-hormonal backup method such as condoms during treatment and for one month afterward.
4. Continue levothyroxine. Rifampin can lower levothyroxine levels, so recheck TSH in 6 to 8 weeks.
5. She should call for nausea, abdominal pain, dark urine, or yellow eyes, and liver tests should be repeated if any of these occur.
6. Report to the county health department, which will arrange monthly clinic monitoring.
7. She may be discharged from the emergency department with infectious disease clinic follow-up in 2 weeks.
summary: A 46-year-old female home health aide with a positive interferon-gamma release assay was seen in the emergency department with a Spanish interpreter for evaluation of latent tuberculosis infection. She had a mild dry cough for two weeks but denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Vital signs and examination were normal, the chest radiograph was clear, and liver enzymes, HIV antibody, and hepatitis B and C tests were normal or negative. The impression was latent tuberculosis infection with a low likelihood of active disease, and the plan is two sputum AFB samples, then rifampin 600 mg daily for four months once smears are negative, with contraception counseling, a TSH recheck, and health department reporting.

note: Dictating a follow-up visit in the celiac clinic for a 70-year-old male with celiac disease diagnosed two years ago. He comes in today for routine follow-up, and he tells me he is trying to follow the gluten-free diet but has been struggling since he lost his wife last year. He lives alone, he has no family in the area, and the only help he has is a neighbor who occasionally drives him to appointments. He does his own shopping and cooking, he relies a lot on canned soups and frozen dinners, and he is not sure which of them contain gluten. He estimates that he gets glutened about once a week. He denies diarrhea, abdominal pain, and blood in the stool, and he has had no rash and no unintentional weight loss. He feels a bit more fatigued than last year. Past medical history includes hypertension and osteopenia found on his last bone density scan. Current medications are lisinopril 10 mg daily, vitamin D3 1000 international units daily, and a calcium supplement 500 mg twice daily. No known drug allergies. On exam his blood pressure is 132/76, heart rate 68, and weight 68 kilograms, correction, 72 kilograms, which is up from 70 kilograms at his last visit. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, and not distended with normal bowel sounds. There are no oral aphthous ulcers, no skin rash, and no edema. Labs from last week show hemoglobin 12.1, ferritin 14 which is low, and vitamin D 22 which is low. The tissue transglutaminase IgA was 38, correction, 58, down from 120 at diagnosis but still elevated. My impression is celiac disease with persistent serologic activity from ongoing inadvertent gluten exposure, iron deficiency anemia, vitamin D insufficiency, osteopenia, and hypertension that is stable. Because he is a 70-year-old male with iron deficiency anemia, I also want to exclude a colonic source of blood loss. For the plan, I am starting ferrous sulfate 325 mg every other day, increasing the vitamin D3 to 2000 international units daily, and continuing the calcium and lisinopril. I am referring him to a dietitian who specializes in celiac disease, and to social work for help with gluten-free meal delivery and transportation, since he lives alone with limited support. I am ordering a colonoscopy, and social work will also help him arrange a ride and an escort for the procedure. We will repeat the tissue transglutaminase IgA, hemoglobin, and ferritin in three months and I will repeat the bone density scan in one year. Return to clinic in three months, sooner if he develops diarrhea, black stools, or weight loss. End of dictation.

Ferrous sulfate was started, vitamin D3 was increased to 2000 international units daily, and a colonoscopy, dietitian, and social work referrals were arranged, with repeat labs in three months.

note:
Visit modality: Audio-only telephone visit. The patient was at home in a private room, her identity was confirmed with two identifiers, and she gave verbal consent for telephone care.

Reason for visit: 42-year-old female with recurrent vulvovaginal itching and discharge.

History per patient: She reports four similar episodes in the past 12 months. This episode began 4 days ago with vulvar itching, burning, and a thick white clumpy discharge without odor. Symptoms started about a week after she finished a 10-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate for sinusitis. She denies fever, pelvic or abdominal pain, dysuria, and unusual vaginal bleeding. She has had no new sexual partners and is in a monogamous relationship. She tried clotrimazole 1% vaginal cream at night for 3 nights with little relief. Prior episodes responded to a single dose of fluconazole but returned within 6 to 8 weeks. A wet mount at her last visit three months ago showed yeast, and the culture grew Candida albicans. Her A1c two months ago was 6.1%, in the prediabetes range. She also takes loratadine 10 mg daily for seasonal allergic rhinitis. No known drug allergies.

Home-measured data: She took her temperature this morning and it was 98.4 F. No other home vital signs are available.

Exam: None, because this was a telephone visit and no visual exam was possible.

Impression: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, with four or more episodes in 12 months, probably triggered by the recent antibiotic course, with prediabetes as a contributing risk factor. Bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, and sexually transmitted infection are less likely given the discharge description and no new partners, but they cannot be excluded by phone.

Management: Stop the clotrimazole cream. Start fluconazole 150 mg by mouth on day 1, day 4, and day 7, then 150 mg once weekly for 6 months as suppressive therapy. She will come in within 1 week for a pelvic exam, vaginal pH, wet mount, and yeast culture. Repeat A1c and fasting glucose with her next labs. Advised her to wear cotton underwear and to avoid douching and scented products. She should call for fever, pelvic pain, foul-smelling discharge, or no improvement in 72 hours. Follow-up call in 1 week.

She denied fever, pelvic or abdominal pain, dysuria, and unusual vaginal bleeding, and over-the-counter clotrimazole cream gave little relief. A prior wet mount and culture showed Candida albicans, and her A1c two months ago was 6.1%. The impression was recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis with prediabetes as a risk factor. Clotrimazole was stopped, fluconazole 150 mg was started with weekly suppression for 6 months, and an in-person pelvic exam and testing were arranged within one week.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. So you're a 79-year-old female and you were sent over because a nodule was found on your thyroid. Tell me how you found out.
Patient: My regular doctor ordered an ultrasound of my neck to look at the artery in my neck, the carotid. They said they saw a little lump in my thyroid by accident. I've been worried sick about cancer ever since.
Doctor: I understand. That is a common worry, but most thyroid nodules turn out to be benign. Let me ask you some questions. Have you noticed a lump in your neck yourself?
Patient: No, I can't feel anything.
Doctor: Any pain in the neck, trouble swallowing, or hoarseness?
Patient: No pain, no trouble swallowing, and my voice is the same.
Doctor: Any shortness of breath when you lie flat?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Any palpitations, shakiness, heat intolerance, or weight loss?
Patient: None of those. My weight is steady, actually.
Doctor: Have you ever had radiation to your head or neck, or does anyone in the family have thyroid cancer?
Patient: No radiation, and no one with thyroid cancer.
Doctor: What medicines do you take?
Patient: Amlodipine 5 mg every morning for my blood pressure, alendronate 70 mg once a week for my bones, and biotin 5000 mcg a day for my hair and nails.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Your vitals are blood pressure 138/74 and heart rate 70. On exam, the right side of your thyroid has a firm nodule about 1.5 to 2 centimeters that moves with swallowing. The left lobe feels normal. There are no enlarged lymph nodes in your neck, and there's no tenderness. Your ultrasound report shows a 1.6 centimeter solid, hypoechoic nodule in the right lobe with smooth margins and no calcifications, which is a TI-RADS 4 category, meaning moderately suspicious. Your TSH last month was 1.4, which is normal, so the gland is neither overactive nor underactive.
Patient: Is it cancer?
Doctor: We don't know yet. The risk is lowish but not zero, and the only way to tell is a needle biopsy. So the working problem is a solitary right thyroid nodule with normal thyroid function. I recommend an ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration. It's a quick office procedure with a numbing shot and a very small needle. Given your health, you're a good candidate, and the result will tell us whether we simply watch it or discuss surgery. One more thing: the biotin can interfere with thyroid blood tests, so please stop it now and stay off it for at least 3 days before we repeat the TSH and free T4.
Patient: I'll stop it.
Doctor: Continue the amlodipine for your hypertension and the alendronate for your osteoporosis. We'll schedule the biopsy within two weeks and I'll see you after the result.
Patient: Thank you, Doctor.
summary: A 79-year-old female was referred for a thyroid nodule found incidentally on a neck ultrasound done for the carotid artery, and she denied neck pain, trouble swallowing, hoarseness, palpitations, heat intolerance, and weight loss. Blood pressure was 138/74, a firm right-sided nodule was palpable without enlarged lymph nodes, and ultrasound showed a 1.6 centimeter solid hypoechoic nodule with smooth margins classified as TI-RADS 4. TSH last month was normal at 1.4. The impression was a solitary right thyroid nodule with normal thyroid function, and an ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration will be scheduled within two weeks. Biotin was stopped because it can interfere with thyroid blood tests, and amlodipine and alendronate continue.

Pulmonary medicine follow-up dictation on hospital day 3 for a 69-year-old female with COPD who was admitted with an acute exacerbation and is being seen to set up her maintenance regimen before discharge. She is a former smoker with about 40 pack-years who quit 5 years ago. She tells me she was prescribed Trelegy Ellipta, one inhalation daily, but she stopped using it about two months ago because it costs too much on her fixed income, and for the month before that she was stretching it by using it every other day. Since then she has used only her albuterol inhaler, up to six times a day, and she ran out of it 4 days before admission. She came in with 3 days of worsening dyspnea, increased cough, and more sputum that was yellow. Today she says her breathing is better and she is coughing less. She denies fever, chest pain, leg swelling, and hemoptysis. Her only other medication is amlodipine 5 mg daily for hypertension. She has no known drug allergies.

Current inpatient treatment is prednisone 40 mg daily, day 3 of 5, doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, day 3 of 5, albuterol nebulizer as needed, and 2 liters of oxygen by nasal cannula, which we are weaning. Vitals this morning: temperature 36.9 Celsius, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 20, blood pressure 130/78, and oxygen saturation 93% on 2 liters. On exam she is sitting upright and speaking in full sentences, with a prolonged expiratory phase and scattered end-expiratory wheezes, no accessory muscle use, no crackles, and no leg edema. Labs show a white blood cell count of 11.4, which is expected on steroids, eosinophils 320, and bicarbonate 29. The chest x-ray shows hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms and no infiltrate. Her most recent outpatient spirometry showed an FEV1 of 42 percent of predicted, correction, 38 percent of predicted.

My impression is COPD with an acute exacerbation that was precipitated by cost-related non-adherence to her maintenance inhaler. The eosinophil count above 300 supports keeping an inhaled corticosteroid in her regimen. Since she cannot afford Trelegy, I am stopping it and starting a lower-cost generic budesonide-formoterol inhaler, 160/4.5 mcg, two puffs twice a day, and she will continue albuterol as needed. I have asked the pharmacist and social work to screen her for the manufacturer assistance program and extra help with drug costs, and to fill her prescriptions before she leaves the hospital. I will teach inhaler technique with a spacer and have her demonstrate it back. She will complete the prednisone and doxycycline courses, and I would like her to be weaned to room air and pass a walking oxygen test before discharge. I am referring her to pulmonary rehabilitation, and she will see me in the clinic in two weeks. I also recommend that her pneumococcal vaccination status be confirmed. End of dictation.
